sources.entry: _Libraries for scientific computing. Also see Python-for-Scientists._

summary.one_liner: A curated, sectioned list of Python libraries, tools and learning resources aimed at students and researchers in the sciences.
summary.what_it_does: This is an awesome-style link list rather than a software project. It is organized into topic sections such as Algebra, Numerical Data, Plotting, Visualisation, Parallelization, Testing, Package Management and Workflow, each with a short description and one-line entries for libraries or tutorials. Entries cover tools like NumPy, SciPy, pandas, xarray, Dask, matplotlib, SymPy, pytest and Jupyter, plus domain packages such as astropy, MetPy, SunPy and QuTiP. It also includes a Beginner Recommendations section that suggests an order for getting started. The list states it deliberately omits things scientists are unlikely to need, such as authentication, databases, networking and NLP.
use_cases: find a Python library for a scientific domain
choose tools for numerical computing and data analysis
set up a beginner scientific Python environment
find testing and code quality tools for research code
speed up or parallelize scientific Python code
notable: Sectioned by task (algebra, plotting, parallelization, testing, and so on) rather than alphabetically
Domain-specific section covering astronomy, climate, seismology, neuroscience, quantum and plasma physics
Includes a Beginner Recommendations section with a suggested learning order
Some tools appear under several sections where they fit multiple uses
Derived from and complementary to vinta/awesome-python
caveats: It is a list of links and short descriptions, not installable software, so entries are not verified or maintained as code here
Some listed resources are dated; the README notes the visualisation section reflects the state as of early 2020
Some entries are tutorials or articles rather than libraries
keywords: list of python libraries for physics
find python libraries for data analysis
